The formal lesson comes easier once the sounds and patterns already feel familiar. 🌱

Say a word. They echo it. Now say it in a silly voice — robot, whisper, opera.
Take turns. Add a new word each round. First one to giggle loses.
That's it. That's early English practice.

Grammar workbooks have a pacing problem — go too fast and kids memorize without understanding, go too slow and they lose the thread entirely.
The design challenge is finding the rhythm that lets a concept land before the next one arrives.
That balance is what I kept coming back to while building Little Learners' English Grammar.

Kids learning to build sentences aren't thinking about grammar — they're thinking about whether what they said sounds right.
That instinct for rightness, that tiny pause before they try again, is doing more work than any rule ever could.
You can teach around it. But you can't skip it.

ESL grammar is tricky to sequence — not because the rules are complicated, but because the order you introduce them changes everything.
Teach articles before nouns are solid and kids just memorize without anchoring. Flip it, and suddenly the rule has something to stick to.
That sequencing problem is basically the whole design puzzle behind Little Learners' English Grammar.

The whole structure of Little Words, Big Discoveries came from sitting with that tension.

Draw three cards. Build a sentence using one word from each category.
No writing required. Just talking, laughing, and quietly building grammar sense. 🃏
